2.text: Besides the boots and shoes already described, the Reindeer and Maritime

3.text: Chukchee have the so-called “dry boots” (keˊrg̣ɪ-pčeˊkɪt), which are worn at

4.text: home when resting from the fatigue of travel and work. These boots are of

5.text: various shapes. One of the most common forms has the legs made of thin slick

6.text: reindeer-leg skin, and the feet of brown, smoked, and curried retteˊm leather.¹

7.text: The tops of these are trimmed with narrow strips of crimson-dyed seal-skin

8.text: or red cloth. Others are made entirely of curried leather and adorned with

9.text: rude embroidery (Fig. 181, b, c). The “dry boots” of women (Fig. 181, d)

10.text: bear a close resemblance to the patterns used by the Koryak, the Kamchadal,

11.text: and the Russianized Yukaghir. This form of boot thus appears to be spread

13.text: With most forms of summer boots the strings are attached in the same

14.text: way as among the Alaskan Eskimo. They are fastened to both sides of the

15.text: instep, and in tying are crossed in front, passed through two loops placed on

16.text: each side of the boot near the sole, then crossed behind the heel and wound

17.text: around the ankle, and finally tied in front. This method of fastening the

18.text: strings is used for curried reindeer-skin shoes of the Reindeer herdsmen, for

19.text: seal-skin boots of the Maritime hunters, and, among the Koryak, on “dry

20.text: shoes” and short summer boots made of retteˊm.

21.text: Mittens (Fig. 182) for summer use are made of seal-skin or curried retteˊm

22.text: leather, and are similar in shape to those worn in winter.

23.text: Gloves of curried leather are sometimes worn, but are

24.text: probably copied after Russian and Lamut patterns.

25.text: Caps are made either of the thinnest leg-skins of fawns

26.text: or of curried leather. Large hoods of the latter material,

27.text: similar in shape to the storm-hoods for winter use, are

28.text: worn for protection from insects. They are often trimmed

29.text: with leather fringe around the face and all along the

31.text: In the spring-time the herdsmen wear light caps with-

32.text: out crowns (Fig. 183, a). These are more common in

33.text: the inland camps. The Maritime young men, while foot-

34.text: racing and indulging in other athletic exercises, sometimes

35.text: wear crownless caps of a somewhat different pattern (Fig.

36.text: 183, b). A third style is worn by Lamut hunters. This

37.text: combines the crownless cap with a protector for cheeks

38.text: and chin. The illustration (Fig. 183, c) represents a cap

39.text: of this last style, seen from the front. Two leather bands

40.text: — one running across the fore-head, and the other passing under the nose —
